performers: Hochschulsymphonieorchester, University of Music and Theatre Munich; Marcus Bosch, conductor
intro: The third movement of Bruckner’s Symphony No. 7 is a scherzo in A minor, in which a trumpet call sounds over a figure in the strings. In the trio between the scherzo’s two fast sections, the violins play a broad tune in F major, and the trumpet’s rhythm is still heard.

sections.label: A · Trumpet call over string figuration
sections.mNote: The A minor scherzo uses an octave leap and repeated notes.

sections.label: B · Winds alternate with strings
sections.mNote: The short figures pass between instruments and appear in inversion.

sections.label: C · Trio, violin melody in F major
sections.mNote: Soft timpani introduce the slower trio.

sections.label: A · Scherzo reprise with trumpet call
sections.mNote: The opening string figure returns at the original fast tempo.

sections.label: Coda · Strings and brass, A minor
sections.mNote: Repeated figures continue to the final chord.

relations.label: The scherzo returns after the trio
relations.basis: The score’s da capo restores the scherzo after its F-major trio. The 326 s measured offset agrees with the opening and the return marked near 328 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.973, sustained 195.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 326 s (cache/form/bruckner-7-scherzo.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening, trumpet and strings
cues.text: The strings repeat a compact figure. After four bars a solo trumpet enters with an octave leap and a sharply pointed rhythm, and the clarinet follows. The string figure continues underneath.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), III, opening, printed p. 51. The four-bar string introduction is also described by the Munich analysis: https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Inversion of the scherzo figures
cues.text: The strings resume quietly and the winds follow in longer phrases. Bruckner inverts the short figures and passes them between high and low instruments.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, letter D, p. 57. Inversions in the scherzo’s contrasting section are illustrated in the Munich analysis cited above.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition of the Scherzo, 1882
cues.text: Bruckner wrote this Scherzo before he had finished the first movement. He completed the sketch by 14 July 1882 and scored it between 12 August and 16 October. He composed the Adagio after the Scherzo.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording of the Seventh (2023): Scherzo and Trio sketched by 14 July 1882 and scored 12 August – 16 October 1882, before the first movement was completed; the Adagio composed after the Scherzo. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Trio in F major
cues.text: Soft timpani introduce the trio. First violins play a long F major melody, marked gesangvoll (songful), over a held bass. The tempo is slower, and the trumpet’s pointed rhythm returns among the violin phrases.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, Trio, p. 66: Etwas langsamer, timpani introduction, gesangvoll violins, F pedal and trumpet entry.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ringtheater fire, 1881
cues.text: On 8 December 1881, Vienna’s Ringtheater burned across the street from Bruckner’s home. Afraid the fire would spread, he gathered his manuscripts. The following day he saw the bodies of victims being carried away, and he described the disaster in a letter to his brother-in-law.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs relates the Ringtheater fire, Bruckner’s response and his letter to Johann Nepomuk Hueber the following Sunday. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Cohrs on the Trio and the Ringtheater
cues.text: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs heard the trio as a picture of the audience in the Ringtheater before the fire. He described it as a lyrical waltz in F major, innocent and intimate, introduced by ghostly timpani, with the people in the stalls in a happy mood and unaware that anything was wrong.
cues.evidence: Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording of the Seventh (2023), on the Trio and the Ringtheater fire: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Scherzo da capo
cues.text: The trio ends in F major. After the pause, the quick string figure in A minor returns, followed by the trumpet call. Bruckner asks for the whole scherzo again, including its quiet wind exchanges and brass entries.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, end of Trio, p. 70: Scherzo Da Capo; return to p. 51.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cohrs on the returning Scherzo
cues.text: Cohrs read the returning Scherzo as a fire, with the strings’ figure as flames. The trumpet call, long heard as a cock-crow, may in his view be the “red cock”, a folk expression for flames on a burning roof.
cues.evidence: Cohrs, Hyperion booklet note: the string accompaniment derived from the first movement’s third theme as flames, the trumpet call often read as “Kikeriki” and possibly the “red cock” or “firebird” of folk speech. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: First performance, Leipzig, 1884
cues.text: Arthur Nikisch conducted the première of the Seventh with the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig on 30 December 1884, when Bruckner was sixty. His symphonies had met hostile receptions for years. This performance was a public triumph.
cues.evidence: Premiere and reception: Thomas May, St. Louis Symphony, https://slso.org/bruckners-seventh/; Berlin Philharmonic, https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-7-in-e-major/

cues.title: End of the scherzo, A minor
cues.text: Woodwind and brass join the strings’ repeated figure. Trumpets carry the opening rhythm forward, and trombones, tuba and timpani reinforce the final climb. The scherzo ends in A minor with the whole orchestra playing together.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, final pages of the scherzo, pp. 60–65, repeated after the Trio.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Timpani open the trio
transitions.to: C · Trio, violin melody in F major
transitions.how: The scherzo ends with the full orchestra in A minor. After the rests the timpani play alone, softly, at the slower Etwas langsamer. The first violins then enter with the F major trio melody, marked gesangvoll. Beneath it the inner strings hold sustained notes, the cellos move and the basses hold an F.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), III, scherzo ending and Trio opening, pp. 65–66.

transitions.title: Trio’s F major close to A minor scherzo
transitions.from: C · Trio, violin melody in F major
transitions.to: A · Scherzo reprise with trumpet call
transitions.how: Flute, oboe and clarinet finish the trio above held F major chords in the strings, and the horn plays the scherzo’s rhythm. The phrase drops to pianissimo and stops. At Scherzo Da Capo the fast A minor string figure returns, followed by the solo trumpet’s octave call.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, III, Trio ending, p. 70, and scherzo opening, p. 51.

source.title: Bruckner, Symphony No. 7, full score (Vienna: A. J. Gutmann, 1885, plate A.J.G. 576; first edition)
source.locator: III. Scherzo, printed pp. 51–65; Trio, pp. 66–70. Scherzo Da Capo returns to the opening.

timeline.note: All five string groups repeat the quiet A-minor figure.
A solo trumpet gives the octave call; clarinet answers above the strings.
Woodwinds and horns join in a crescendo; trumpets rest.
Tutti fortissimo: brass, tuba and a timpani roll over rushing strings.
Quieter section: flute, oboe and clarinet play the melody, with solos for horn and trumpet over the strings.
A soft brass chorale; trombones and tuba swell with the winds.
Oboe, clarinet, bassoon and horn exchange solos above plucked cellos and basses.
A crescendo builds in winds, horns and trumpets over the strings.
Second tutti at fortissimo with trombones, tuba and timpani.
Mezzo-forte wind and horn phrases with a trumpet solo; trombones and timpani rest.
Final build: trombones, tuba and timpani rejoin, and the music stays fortissimo to the end of the scherzo.
Soft timpani introduce the trio; the first violins enter with their melody over a held bass F.
Horn and trumpet solos over the strings.
Flute, oboe and clarinet take the melody over strings, with one horn.
A pianissimo brass chorale with soft timpani; the strings enter at the close.
The trio rises to forte, with the brass joining strings and winds, then grows quieter again.
All five string groups return to the quiet A-minor figure.
The solo trumpet’s octave call returns, answered by clarinet.
Woodwinds and horns join in a crescendo; trumpets rest.
Tutti fortissimo again, with brass, tuba and timpani.
Softer wind melody with horn and trumpet solos over strings.
Soft brass chorale swelling with the winds.
Wind and horn solos return above plucked cellos and basses.
The closing section begins with a crescendo in the woodwind, horns and trumpets.
Second tutti at fortissimo with trombones, tuba and timpani.
Mezzo-forte wind and horn phrases; trombones and timpani rest.
The final build to the closing fortissimo of the whole orchestra.

composer.epithet: Composer who studied his craft for half his life before writing symphonies in which a horn call can expand into full brass.
facts: St Florian; counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; composition with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz; Vienna Conservatory from 1868; university lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two outside the sequence; masses, motets and secular choral music
The Seventh Symphony, Leipzig, 30 December 1884; Arthur Nikisch conducting
composer.background:
On 16 December 1877 Bruckner conducted his Third Symphony with the Vienna Philharmonic. Johann Herbeck, who had intended to conduct it, had died in October. The audience began to leave during the performance. Among the supporters who stayed was the seventeen-year-old Mahler, who helped arrange the large score for piano duet. Bruckner was then fifty-three, a professor at the conservatory and an organist admired internationally. As a symphonist he was still little known in the concert hall.

He was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father taught school and played church music. After his father died in 1837, his mother took him to the Augustinian abbey of St Florian as a choirboy. He learned the organ, trained as a teacher and worked in the villages of Windhaag and Kronstorf. In Windhaag he also played the fiddle for dancing.
